changedBeliefs: The `Isolate.exit` sacrifice policy (kill the reader to zero-copy a >=256 KB result heap instead of paying the SendPort graph copy) was re-evaluated against the Dart 2.15 isolate-group send model, where SendPort.send SHARES immutable leaves (strings/ints/canonical) and only COPIES the mutable structural graph. Confirmed transport model (`native_vs_heap_send.dart`): send cost tracks the mutable/copyable payload — a heap Uint8List send blows up with size (203-272 us at 512-731 KB) while a native-backed view sends cheaply (23-44 us). So send is cheap exactly when the result is immutable-heavy (text) or externally backed, and expensive only for large mutable structure.

Sacrifice-vs-send crossover (A/B via a reverted RESQLITE_SACRIFICE_THRESHOLD define): on a numeric lane (structure-only, slots = rows x cols) send is faster-or-level up to ~20k slots and sacrifice edges ahead only above ~32k slots by a noisy ~3-4% (2000/8000/20000/32000/48000 slots: sacrifice 76.8/238.6/976.5/1194.8/1856.3 vs send 72.3/226.3/931.9/1233.8/1932.6). On a text lane (200 B strings) send wins everywhere and large (1000 rows: 149.4 vs 438.3 us) because strings are shared on send while sacrifice pays a respawn for a copy it never needed. The crossover metric is STRUCTURAL SLOT COUNT, not bytes.

Neither candidate change survives. Retiring sacrifice (send-always) is rejected because send-always would regress the high-structural-count tail (>= ~32k slots) where sacrifice still wins. Re-triggering on structural slot count instead of estimated bytes is rejected because the crossover sits at a high slot count with a ~3-4% noisy margin and estimated bytes already correlates with slot count for structural results — the accounting complexity isn't paid for. Current 256 KB estimated-byte policy stands unchanged.

Measurement confound identified: within one process the repeated sacrifice respawns accumulate and interfere, so a per-process A/B cannot cleanly isolate a single sacrifice-vs-send at a fixed size — it biases the sacrifice lane by respawn history. This is why the send-vs-sacrifice signal has stayed muddy across exp 241's harnesses (and why the stranded `sacrifice_reeval_ab.dart`, which also lost its `debugReaderSpawnCount` counter to exp 236's cleanup, could not resolve it).
nextSignals: Peer-recommended resolution (2026-07-22) is a two-experiment estimand SPLIT, not one better harness. Do NOT try to build a single benchmark that isolates transfer, preserves realistic pool lifecycle, includes decode, and avoids heap-state effects — those are different estimands and forcing them together is what produced this run's sign-unstable median. Experiment A (prepared-result handoff): fresh AOT process per observation, real ResultSet built BEFORE a Go-barrier, measure Go-sent-on-main -> raw result-handler-entered-on-main, ABBA-matched send vs exit children; record receive time as the FIRST op in the handler (the sync completer runs downstream work otherwise). Experiment B (pool burst): production 4-worker pool, 8 identical large-row requests behind a barrier, measure queue-wait (workerAssignedAt - requestEnqueuedAt) for requests 5-8, reset pool between bursts, three lanes send / sacrifice-current / sacrifice-eager-respawn. Conclude both with equivalence testing (TOST) against a pre-registered margin, not by waiting for a noisy median to acquire a sign.

CONFIRMED lifecycle lead (highest leverage): `ReaderPool._WorkerSlot`'s reply handler completes the pending request (a `Completer.sync()`, so `complete()` runs the whole `_dispatch`/`_requery`/`entry.emit`/`_flushQueue` chain synchronously) BEFORE initiating the replacement via `unawaited(spawn(...))` in the sacrifice branch — whereas the sibling non-sacrifice branch deliberately calls `_notifyPool()` BEFORE completing. So the replacement launch is delayed by arbitrary caller work; sacrifice's pool-capacity cost may be an artifact of launch ordering, not the transfer policy. Experiment B must include a sacrifice-eager-respawn lane (start the spawn before completing the caller, with `_closed`/slot-generation guards so a late replacement self-terminates on a closed pool). If eager respawn erases the queue-wait penalty, the fix is launch ordering, not the sacrifice threshold.

Clean standalone win independent of the middle-numeric question: the TEXT/shared-leaf misroute. Sacrifice fires on a 256 KB BYTE threshold, but shared-string results send ~2.9x cheaper than they sacrifice (strings share on send; sacrifice respawns for a copy that never happens). A routing guard that keeps shared-leaf-dominated results on send is shippable now and does not depend on resolving send-vs-sacrifice for mutable structure. The byte threshold is a proxy; the real cost driver is the MUTABLE structural slot count.

General result-transfer-shape rule reinforced: send is cheap for immutable-heavy (shared leaves) and native/external-backed content, expensive only for large mutable structure. Sacrifice can only pay off when the mutable structural graph is large enough that its copy exceeds a reader respawn AND the replacement launch is not itself the bottleneck — a narrow regime that experiments A/B must pin before any retune.
